report_title: Tropic Trooper (KeyBoy / Pirate Panda / Earth Centaur) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction (2024 Middle East government campaign)
source: Kaspersky Securelist 'New macro-free web shell from the Tropic Trooper group is found in the Middle East' (Sherif Magdy, 2024-09-06, https://securelist.com/new-tropic-trooper-web-shell-infection/113737/); Kaspersky press 'Tropic Trooper APT broadens target scope with new cyberespionage campaigns in Middle East' (2024, https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/tropic-trooper-apt-broadens-target-scope-with-new-cyberespionage-campaigns-in-middle-east); Trend Micro 'Collecting In the Dark: Tropic Trooper Targets Transportation and Government Organizations' / Earth Centaur (2021-12, https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/21/l/collecting-in-the-dark-tropic-trooper-targets-transportation-and-government-organizations.html); MITRE ATT&CK Group Tropic Trooper G0081 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0081/)

actor.name: Tropic Trooper
related_clusters: Crowdoor loader (variant of the SparrowDoor backdoor, ESET Sept 2021)
Historic backdoors: ChiserClient, SmileSvr, Gh0stCringe/USBFerry (Earth Centaur reporting)
actor.attribution: China-nexus cyber-espionage group active since at least 2011, assessed Chinese-speaking based on code artifacts, tooling (China Chopper, Fscan, Neo-reGeorg, Godzilla, mimikatz-via-Swor) and target selection aligned with PRC strategic interest. Kaspersky and Trend Micro track it as Tropic Trooper / Earth Centaur; MITRE catalogs it as G0081. Attribution to a China-nexus state-aligned actor is medium-to-high confidence (converging vendor assessments, tradecraft and victimology) but no single government advisory names a specific PRC entity, so specific-unit attribution remains unconfirmed.
targeted_regions_mena: Middle East (regional human-rights subject matter targeted via a Malaysian study)
targeted_sectors: Government (human-rights / studies related to the Middle East)

key_campaigns.name: Middle East government entity — Umbraco China Chopper web shell + Crowdoor loader
key_campaigns.summary: Persistent intrusion into a Middle East government entity's public-facing Umbraco (open-source .NET CMS) web server. Kaspersky telemetry flagged recurring alerts for a new China Chopper web-shell variant compiled as a .NET Umbraco module (App_Web_*.dll dropped into the ASP.NET Temporary Files tree, EnableEventValidation=false, multi-stage Base64 decoding). Post-exploitation used Fscan, Swor (mimikatz/FRP/ElevationStation), Neo-reGeorg SOCKS5 pivoting and ByPassGodzilla. The intrusion delivered the Crowdoor loader (a SparrowDoor backdoor variant) via DLL side-loading of legitimate signed binaries (inst.exe, WinStore.exe) loading malicious DLLs (VERSION.dll, datast.dll, datastate.dll) with RC4-decrypted shellcode (key fYTUdr643$3u) injected into colorcpl.exe. Persistence via a Windows service (WinStore) with an HKCU Run-key fallback; HTTPS C2 to blog.techmersion[.]com:443. A new web-shell variant carried defense-evasion updates to bypass detection.

key_campaigns.name: Earth Centaur — transportation & government (ProxyShell/IIS)
key_campaigns.summary: Long-running espionage against transportation companies and transportation-related government agencies. Initial access via vulnerable Microsoft Exchange (ProxyLogon/ProxyShell) and IIS servers, followed by China Chopper web shells and custom backdoors (ChiserClient, SmileSvr, Gh0stCringe). Actor sought internal documents (flight schedules, financial planning) and personal data; used DLL side-loading, living-off-the-land discovery and encrypted C2.

ttps.procedure_description: Actor probes internet-facing servers for exploitable web applications and CMS/Exchange/ColdFusion vulnerabilities prior to exploitation; public-facing server scanning precedes deployment of the China Chopper web shell.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — pre-compromise scanning of public-facing servers happens off-victim/at the perimeter and rarely attributes to this actor; hunt/external-attack-surface candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Actor registers and operates espionage C2 domains such as techmersion[.]com (subdomain blog.techmersion[.]com) used for the Crowdoor backdoor's HTTPS command-and-control.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — adversary domain registration/staging is off-victim; intel/infrastructure-tracking candidate (pivot on registrant/hosting/TLS)

ttps.procedure_description: Actor develops and maintains custom implants — the Crowdoor loader (a SparrowDoor variant) and updated China Chopper Umbraco web-shell variants carrying defense-evasion improvements — plus historic backdoors ChiserClient and SmileSvr.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — capability development is off-victim; intel candidate. Downstream implant execution is where host detection lands

ttps.procedure_description: Primary initial-access vector: exploitation of a public-facing open-source Umbraco (.NET) CMS web server to plant a China Chopper web shell. Earlier/related intrusions exploited Microsoft Exchange ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207) and Adobe ColdFusion (CVE-2023-26360), and IIS/Exchange servers (Earth Centaur).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — exploitation of internet-facing CMS/Exchange/ColdFusion is a strong detection surface: web-server/WAF logs, anomalous POSTs to CMS endpoints, exploit signatures for the named CVEs, and new DLL/script artifacts written into the web root and ASP.NET temporary-files tree

ttps.procedure_description: Actor deploys a China Chopper variant compiled as a .NET Umbraco CMS module, written as App_Web_{8-char}[a-z0-9].dll into c:\microsoft.net\framework64\v4.0.30319\temporary asp.net files\root\...; the module disables event validation (EnableEventValidation=false) and performs multiple Base64 decodings before generating and executing the final JavaScript payload. Provides durable command execution on the compromised web server; Godzilla/ByPassGodzilla web shells also used.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — new App_Web_*.dll modules and web-shell files appearing in the Umbraco/ASP.NET temporary-files tree, w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe/powershell, and web-shell request patterns are high-fidelity file-integrity and process-lineage detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Actor runs commands through the web shell and drops a batch script (i.bat) to perform ICMP ping reconnaissance, writing output to text files for targeting.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — cmd.exe/batch execution spawned by the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) and ping-sweep loops writing enumeration output are detectable via process command-line and process-lineage telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: The Crowdoor loader resolves and calls native Windows APIs to decrypt (RC4) and execute shellcode in memory and to perform process injection, minimizing on-disk footprint.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — direct native-API use is generic and hard to isolate without deep memory/EDR telemetry; hunt candidate correlated with side-load and injection events

ttps.procedure_description: Actor executes the loaded payload via a Windows service (service name WinStore), and Fscan/tooling launches remote execution during lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — service-based execution (services.exe spawning an unusual image) is detectable via service-install and process-lineage telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttps.procedure_description: Crowdoor establishes persistence by creating a Windows service named WinStore that launches the side-loaded loader; if service creation fails it falls back to a registry Run-key ASEP.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — new service creation (Event ID 7045) named WinStore pointing at a non-standard binary path is a high-fidelity, actor-relevant detection

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: Fallback persistence: Crowdoor writes an auto-start extensibility point at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with value name WinStore when service creation is not possible.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — creation of an HKCU...\Run value named WinStore referencing a payload in an unusual path is directly observable via registry-modification telemetry (Sysmon EID 13)

ttps.procedure_description: Core stealth technique: DLL side-loading / search-order hijacking. Legitimate signed binaries (inst.exe, WinStore.exe) are placed alongside malicious DLLs (VERSION.dll, datast.dll, datastate.dll) dropped to c:\Windows\branding\data and c:\Users\Public\Music\data so the trusted EXE loads the attacker DLL, which RC4-decrypts (key fYTUdr643$3u) and runs the Crowdoor shellcode. datast.dll exports InitCore (older) and Ldf/rcd (updated); datastate.dll exports Clear/Server.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — a signed binary loading an unsigned VERSION.dll/datast.dll from c:\Windows\branding\data or c:\Users\Public\Music\data is detectable via module-load (Sysmon EID 7) signature-mismatch and path-anomaly analytics; the exact DLL names/paths are actor-specific IOCs

ttps.procedure_description: The loader injects the decrypted Crowdoor payload into the legitimate Windows binary colorcpl.exe (launched with command-line argument "2") to run under a trusted process context.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — colorcpl.exe spawned with an unusual argument and hosting injected code / making network connections is detectable via process-lineage and cross-process injection (Sysmon EID 8/10) telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Crowdoor shellcode is injected into a benign process (colorcpl.exe) to blend malicious network and execution activity with a signed Windows utility and evade image-based detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — anomalous network/behavior from colorcpl.exe and injected-thread indicators are detectable with EDR, but generic injection needs correlation with the side-load event

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
ttps.procedure_description: Crowdoor shellcode is stored RC4-encrypted (a stream-cipher variant, key fYTUdr643$3u) inside the malicious DLLs and decrypted at runtime; the Umbraco web shell wraps its payload in multiple layers of Base64 encoding.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — high-entropy encrypted blobs embedded in DLLs and multi-layer Base64 web-shell payloads are detectable via file-entropy/YARA scanning, but require dedicated inspection

ttps.procedure_description: At runtime the loader RC4-decrypts embedded shellcode and the web shell performs multiple Base64 decodings before executing the final JavaScript payload.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — in-memory decode routines leave little discrete host signal; hunt candidate alongside side-load/injection correlation

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: Actor names the malicious service and payload WinStore (mimicking Microsoft Store) and drops attacker DLLs named VERSION.dll/datast.dll under legitimate-looking paths such as c:\Windows\branding\data to blend with normal system files.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — legitimate-looking names (WinStore, VERSION.dll) in unusual paths are detectable via name/path/hash baselining and signature-vs-name mismatch

ttps.technique_name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
ttps.procedure_description: Actor stages payloads in obscure data subdirectories (c:\Windows\branding\data, c:\Users\Public\Music\data) to keep implant components out of common inspection paths.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — payloads tucked into uncommon data folders evade casual review; hunt candidate via file-creation telemetry on non-standard directories

ttps.procedure_description: Actor removes intermediate tools and artifacts after use and iterated a new web-shell variant with defense-evasion updates specifically to reduce detection footprint.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — post-op cleanup/file deletion is hard to observe after the fact; hunt candidate via file-deletion auditing and shell-history reconstruction

ttps.procedure_description: The Swor bundle packages ElevationStation and evasion tooling used to bypass endpoint controls; the actor tunes web-shell variants to evade security-product detection during the intrusion.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tampering with or bypassing security tooling is detectable via EDR tamper-protection and security-product health telemetry, but the report gives limited specifics

ttps.procedure_description: Actor deploys mimikatz (delivered inside the Swor tool bundle) to dump credentials from LSASS on compromised hosts to enable privilege escalation and lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — process access to lsass.exe and mimikatz signatures/command lines are highly observable via EDR process-access (Sysmon EID 10) telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Actor runs Fscan to scan the internal network for live hosts, open ports and services to identify lateral-movement targets after establishing a web-shell foothold.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Fscan execution and internal connection-fanout/port-scan bursts are detectable via process command-line and east-west network analytics

ttps.procedure_description: Actor uses the i.bat script to perform ICMP ping sweeps enumerating reachable internal hosts, saving results to text files for targeting.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — scripted ping-sweep loops (repeated ping.exe invocations) and output redirection are detectable via process command-line telemetry within a recon-burst window

ttps.procedure_description: Actor enumerates installed security/AV products on compromised hosts to plan evasion before deploying the Crowdoor loader.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — queries listing AV/EDR services and products are detectable via command-line and API-call telemetry, though common in admin activity

ttps.procedure_description: Actor collects host/system information (OS, architecture, configuration) on compromised servers to tailor payloads and side-load targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — system-info enumeration is common and noisy; hunt candidate within a tight recon-burst process-lineage window

ttps.procedure_description: Actor enumerates network configuration and adjacent hosts on the compromised environment to plan pivoting and proxy placement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — ipconfig/route/arp-style enumeration is ubiquitous; hunt candidate only in recon-burst context

ttps.procedure_description: Fscan is used both for discovery and to identify/exploit vulnerable internal services, supporting lateral movement across the compromised network.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal exploitation attempts surface via service crash/anomaly telemetry and east-west IDS, but require internal instrumentation

ttps.procedure_description: After harvesting credentials, the actor moves laterally to additional Windows hosts using SMB/admin-share remote execution to distribute the loader and tooling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — admin-share access (ADMIN$/C$) and remote file writes/service installs are detectable via Type-3 logons (4624), 5140 share access and 7045 service-install events

ttps.procedure_description: Actor deploys Neo-reGeorg as a SOCKS5 web-shell proxy on compromised web servers to tunnel traffic and pivot deeper into the internal network.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Neo-reGeorg tunneling shows as anomalous web-server child processes and SOCKS-over-HTTP request patterns; detectable via web-shell/process analytics and proxy-behavior heuristics

ttps.procedure_description: Actor uses FRP (fast reverse proxy, delivered via the Swor bundle) and Neo-reGeorg to tunnel command-and-control and internal pivot traffic out of the network.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — FRP/reverse-proxy client execution and persistent outbound tunnels are detectable via process signatures and long-lived/anomalous egress connection analytics

ttps.procedure_description: Crowdoor communicates with its C2 over HTTPS on port 443 to blog.techmersion[.]com; historic Earth Centaur backdoors used HTTP(S) C2 as well.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — outbound HTTPS from an unusual process (injected colorcpl.exe) to blog.techmersion[.]com / techmersion[.]com is detectable via proxy/DNS and process-to-network correlation; the C2 domain is an explicit IOC

ttps.procedure_description: Crowdoor C2 rides TLS/HTTPS (port 443), wrapping command-and-control in encrypted transport to blend with normal web traffic and resist inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — TLS C2 blends with legitimate HTTPS; detectable mainly via JA3/JA4 fingerprinting, destination-domain reputation and process-to-network anomaly correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Actor transfers follow-on tooling (Fscan, Swor, Neo-reGeorg, the Crowdoor loader DLLs and side-load host binaries) onto compromised hosts via the web shell and C2 channel.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — files written to disk by the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) or injected process following network transfer are detectable via file-creation and process-to-network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Actor stages reconnaissance and collected data locally — ping-sweep results written to text files and payload/tooling staged in dedicated data directories prior to use and exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — writing enumeration output/staging files is low-signal; hunt candidate via file-creation patterns in staging directories

ttps.procedure_description: Consistent with Earth Centaur tradecraft, the actor collects and archives internal documents (e.g., flight schedules, financial-planning files) and personal data of interest prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — archive-utility execution producing large/compressed outputs before egress is detectable via process command-line and file-write telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Actor exfiltrates collected documents and credentials over the established encrypted Crowdoor HTTPS C2 channel, consistent with its espionage objective against the Middle East government target.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — outbound data volume anomalies over the C2 channel to the actor domain are detectable via egress-volume analytics and process-to-network correlation

detection_signals: New App_Web_{8-char}.dll modules or web-shell files appearing under c:\microsoft.net\framework64\v4.0.30319\temporary asp.net files\root\... on an Umbraco/IIS server; w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe/powershell/ping.exe (China Chopper web-shell activity)
Umbraco/.NET web-shell payload with EnableEventValidation=false and multi-layer Base64 decoding before executing a JavaScript payload

DLL side-loading: signed inst.exe or WinStore.exe loading an unsigned VERSION.dll / datast.dll / datastate.dll from c:\Windows\branding\data or c:\Users\Public\Music\data (module-load signature mismatch, Sysmon EID 7)
datast.dll exports InitCore or Ldf/rcd; datastate.dll exports Clear/Server — YARA/export-name hunt
colorcpl.exe launched with command-line argument "2", hosting injected code and/or making outbound HTTPS connections (Crowdoor injection target)
Windows service named WinStore (Event ID 7045) or HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run value 'WinStore' referencing a payload in a non-standard path
Batch file i.bat performing ICMP ping sweeps with output redirected to text files (recon burst spawned from the web-shell process)
Fscan, Swor (mimikatz/FRP/ElevationStation), Neo-reGeorg (SOCKS5), Godzilla/ByPassGodzilla tooling execution on servers
mimikatz / LSASS process access (Sysmon EID 10) following web-shell foothold
RC4-encrypted shellcode blobs inside side-loaded DLLs (RC4 key artifact fYTUdr643$3u) — YARA/entropy hunt
Outbound HTTPS (port 443) to blog.techmersion[.]com or techmersion[.]com, or connections to 51.195.37.155 / 162.19.135.182
Exploitation of Microsoft Exchange ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473/34523/31207) or Adobe ColdFusion (CVE-2023-26360) on internet-facing servers as an initial-access precursor
notes: Primary MENA source is Kaspersky GReAT's 2024 report on the Tropic Trooper intrusion into a Middle East government entity (Securelist, Sherif Magdy, 2024-09-06), corroborated by Kaspersky press releases and enriched with Trend Micro's 2021 Earth Centaur reporting and MITRE ATT&CK G0081 for historic TTPs. This actor is in the MENA Detection Library because of the 2024 Middle East government campaign (Umbraco China Chopper web shell + Crowdoor/SparrowDoor loader) and related targeting of a Malaysian study on human rights in the region — a notable geographic expansion from its historic East/Southeast Asia focus. actor.mitre_id intentionally left empty per tasking (public MITRE group id G0081 cited only in source/aliases, not as the actor id). Attribution: China-nexus / Chinese-speaking espionage assessed at medium-to-high confidence by converging vendor reporting (tradecraft + tooling + victimology); no single government advisory names a specific PRC unit, so attribution_confidence is set to 'medium' honestly. ATT&CK normalization to this environment's bundled (reorganized) dataset: Web Shell = T1505.003 (NOTE: in this env T1505.004 is 'IIS Components', NOT web shell — do not substitute); DLL side-loading uses T1574.001 (public T1574.002 absent); Encrypted/Encoded File = T1027.013; Windows Service persistence = T1543.003; registry Run-key = T1547.001; Disable/Modify Tools = T1685 under tactic 'defense-impairment'; Indicator Removal/File Deletion = T1070.004 placed under 'defense-impairment'; defense-evasion techniques use tactic slug 'stealth'. Every technique_id was validated as a key in the environment's bundled attack_dump.json (697 techniques) before inclusion — zero invalid IDs. STRONGEST DETECTION SURFACE (detect, high feasibility): T1190 public-server/CMS exploitation, T1505.003 App_Web_* China Chopper web shell, T1574.001 inst.exe/WinStore.exe -> VERSION.dll/datast.dll side-load, T1543.003/T1547.001 WinStore service+Run-key persistence, T1003.001 mimikatz/LSASS, T1071.001 blog.techmersion[.]com HTTPS C2, T1105 ingress tooling. HUNT-leaning (low feasibility, off-victim/subtle): T1595.002 public-server scanning, T1583.001/T1587.001 infrastructure & malware development, T1140/T1074.001/T1564.001/T1070.004 in-memory decode/staging/hiding/cleanup, T1082/T1016 generic discovery. IOCs are taken verbatim from the Kaspersky Securelist appendix (MD5 web-shell/tool/loader hashes; datast.dll and Umbraco SHA-1/SHA-256; C2 domain techmersion[.]com / blog.techmersion[.]com; C2 IPs 51.195.37.155 and 162.19.135.182; ProxyShell and ColdFusion CVEs). Defang brackets removed for raw machine-readable values per spec; no legitimate/CDN domains were included. Trend Micro's 2021 Earth Centaur report was referenced for historic TTPs but its full IOC appendix could not be retrieved live (HTTP 403), so no unverified Trend Micro indicators were added to the iocs object.
